summary: On Resurrection Sunday the risen Jesus appears to Simon Peter, the disciple who had denied Him. Luke and Paul both record the meeting, but neither describes it.
key_insight: No one tells us what Jesus said to Peter that day. Yet this unrecorded meeting heads Paul’s list of witnesses: “He was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve.” The first apostle to see the risen Lord was the one who had denied Him.
story: Three nights earlier, in the high priest’s courtyard, Simon Peter had denied Jesus three times. When the rooster crowed, he went out and wept bitterly. That morning he had run to the tomb and found only the linen cloths, and he went away marveling at what had happened.

Sometime that same day, the risen Lord appeared to Simon. No one recorded where it happened or what was said. By evening, when the two came back from Emmaus, the disciples in Jerusalem were already saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”

Some twenty-five years later, Paul reminded the Corinthians of the gospel he had passed on to them: Christ died for our sins, was buried and rose the third day, “and that He was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve.”

scene.label: Simon, Cephas, Peter
scene.text: Jesus told Simon at their first meeting, “You shall be called Cephas,” an Aramaic name that John translates “A Stone” (John 1:42). Peter is the same name in Greek. Luke here uses his old name, Simon; Paul usually calls him Cephas.

scene.label: “And Peter”
scene.text: That morning the angel had told the women to carry the news to the disciples “and Peter” (Mark 16:7). Peter was singled out by name before Jesus ever appeared to him.

scene.label: A summary handed on
scene.text: Paul says he “delivered” what he had first “received” (1 Corinthians 15:3), the language of passing on a fixed teaching. Many scholars think this summary was formed within a few years of the resurrection. Paul had spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18).

scene.label: Paul’s list
scene.text: Paul names Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and finally himself. He leaves out the women, whom the Gospels place first, probably because he is giving the kind of public witness list that would carry weight in his day.

witnesses.luke: Luke mentions this appearance only in passing, in the words that greet the travelers from Emmaus, yet it answers something he alone recorded. At the Last Supper Jesus told Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren” (22:32). Here the risen Lord has sought Peter out, and in Acts Peter becomes the strengthener of his brothers.

seeing.reveals: Jesus sought out the disciple who had failed Him most openly, and He met him privately. The risen Lord restores His fallen servants before He sends them out.
seeing.living: Scripture records the fact of this meeting and keeps the conversation private. Peter’s failure had been public, but his first meeting with the risen Jesus was between the two of them. If you carry a failure you cannot undo, bring it to Jesus yourself; He seeks out the one who denied Him.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus met you alone today, what failure would you need to talk with Him about, and do you believe He wants that meeting?

preaching.big_idea: The gospel comes with named witnesses, and the first of them is a forgiven denier.
preaching.watch_for: The phrase “according to the Scriptures” is attached to both the death and the resurrection (15:3–4). Then come the witnesses. Paul grounds the gospel in what Scripture foretold and in people who saw Jesus alive, and the first name on the list is Peter’s.
